title: Operator Sheath: fabric for safely executing community/untrusted admin snippets
creator: Asha Mendes
description: Build a lightweight execution fabric (Operator Sheath) that allows engineers and support to publish, discover, and run small admin snippets contributed internally or from vetted community sources while enforcing resource, data, and permission constraints. The Sheath should provide deterministic dry-run, staged verification, signed artifact verification, RBAC enforcement, telemetry lineage, and an opinionated API surface so snippets can be composed into runbook tasks without granting broad cluster/infra privileges.
background_and_rationale: We frequently need quick, focused scripts (diagnostics, quick-remediations, metadata queries) during incidents and support flows. Today teams either copy ad-hoc scripts or run unsafe playbooks with elevated privileges. This increases blast radius and slows reviews. The Sheath reduces friction by providing a catalog of small, sandboxed microservices (WASM-first) that run with minimal privileges and strong audit trails. This enables faster support while preserving SLOs and compliance controls.
scope: Runtime: WASM sandbox + lightweight policy shim for snippet execution
Signing: artifact signature verification with customer KMS integration for internal CI-signed snippets
Policy: OPA-based allow/deny rules for network, filesystem, and secret access
Dry-run: deterministic dry-run mode that performs validation and smoke checks without side effects
Observability: per-run tracing, token-level cost attribution, and immutable audit event emission to Console
Integrations: Redwood Console UI listing and API endpoint to compose snippets into Linear runbook tasks
out_of_scope: Full container scheduling/VM orchestration (we will not replace Dedicated nodes)
Arbitrary long-running workloads (>15m) — Sheath is for short microactions
User-submitted third-party code execution in production without signature and review
acceptance_criteria: Prototype executes signed WASM snippets with enforced CPU/memory limits and network egress blocked by default
Dry-run returns deterministic smoke-check results and a signed verification bundle
All runs emit structured audit events viewable in Console with run metadata and lineage
RBAC mapping prevents snippets from using high-privilege tokens; attempts are rejected with actionable errors
End-to-end demo: support engineer composes a snippet into a runbook task and triggers a safe staged rollout
design_decisions: Choose WASM as primary execution surface for fast startup, deterministic resource controls, and portable sandboxing
Use OPA Rego policies for allow/deny rules; policies stored alongside snippet metadata and versioned
Sign artifacts in CI using KMS-backed keys; verify signatures at execution time and in the Console UI
Keep the surface minimal: snippets receive a typed input bag and explicit capabilities (eg. kv:read, kv:write) rather than raw credentials
Emit audit events to existing telemetry pipelines (request-level tracing ID + snippet ID) to avoid new stores
tradeoffs_and_risks: WASM sandboxing limits access to native tooling; some legacy admin scripts may need porting — we accept a migration cost
Strict policy defaults increase safety but can slow early adoption; will provide an escape hatch for rapid experiments under a timeboxed approval
Signature+review requirement reduces onboarding velocity for community-contributed snippets; mitigated by a lightweight curated review playbook
implementation_plan: Spike (1 week): prototype WASM runtime wrapper that runs a simple diagnostic snippet and blocks network
MVP (3 sprints): runtime + policy engine + signature verification + Console integration for snippet discovery
Rollout (1 sprint): opt-in beta with two volunteer teams (SRE, Support) and paired docs/templates
GA: expand to Platform and SDK routing with monitoring and rate-limits

open_questions: What is the allowed lifetime for ephemeral credentials issued to snippets (15m vs 1h)?
Do we allow snippets to perform writes to sensitive tables during 'dry-run' in a simulated mode, or require separate staging environments?
Should the default execution tier be rate-limited per-team or per-snippet?
